wrongBelief: A blue circle showing a white bicycle means cycling is banned there.
repairNote: Blue circles are positive orders — here, a route only pedal cycles may use.

wrongBelief: The national speed limit sign means there is no speed limit.
repairNote: It ends local limits: the national limit for your vehicle and road type now applies.

wrongBelief: The national speed limit sign means a maximum of 70 mph on every road.
repairNote: It ends local limits: the national limit for your vehicle and road type now applies.

wrongBelief: With no speed limit signs in sight, you should just drive at whatever feels safe.
repairNote: Street lighting normally means a 30 mph limit applies unless signs show otherwise.

wrongBelief: Driving exactly at the speed limit is always correct because it keeps traffic flowing.
repairNote: Rule 125: the limit is the absolute maximum — it doesn't make that speed safe.

wrongBelief: Overall stopping distance is made up of braking distance only.
repairNote: You travel during your reaction time too — overall = thinking + braking distance.

wrongBelief: On a dry road, one car length behind the vehicle ahead is a safe enough gap.
repairNote: Dry roads: at least two seconds behind the vehicle in front.

wrongBelief: In the wet, a two-second gap — the same as on a dry road — is enough.
repairNote: Wet roads at least double stopping distances — leave at least four seconds.

wrongBelief: The typical overall stopping distance at 70 mph is about 53 metres.
repairNote: At 70 mph you need about 96 m — far more than double the 30 mph distance.

wrongBelief: If someone is tailgating you, you should brake hard to warn them off.
repairNote: Ease back: a bigger gap ahead gives you and the tailgater room to stop safely.

wrongBelief: Modern brakes remove the need for any gap behind the car in front.
repairNote: Thinking distance exists because you travel on while you react — then braking begins.

wrongBelief: Reactions are instant, so you can always react the moment the car in front brakes.
repairNote: Thinking distance exists because you travel on while you react — then braking begins.

wrongBelief: You may cross a solid white centre line to overtake any vehicle slower than you.
repairNote: Exceptions: entering premises or a side road, or passing a cycle, horse or works vehicle at 10 mph or less.

wrongBelief: Double white lines are only advisory, so you may cross them freely.
repairNote: A broken line on your side allows overtaking if you can complete it safely in time.

wrongBelief: A hatched area with solid white borders may be entered any time traffic is slow.
repairNote: Solid borders mean keep out except in an emergency; broken borders mean only if necessary and safe.

wrongBelief: You may wait inside a box junction while queueing straight ahead behind slow traffic.
repairNote: The right-turn wait is the one exception to keeping the box clear.

wrongBelief: A box junction must always stay empty — you may never wait inside one.
repairNote: The right-turn wait is the one exception to keeping the box clear.

wrongBelief: Red reflective studs on your left mark the central reservation.
repairNote: Red = left edge. Amber = right edge, white = lanes, green = slip roads and lay-bys.

wrongBelief: You may enter a box junction whenever the lights are green, whatever the exit looks like.
repairNote: Green light or not: enter the box only when your exit is clear.

wrongBelief: You must use headlights only when other drivers switch theirs on.
repairNote: Unlit roads at night and seriously reduced visibility both require headlights.

wrongBelief: Driving through a lit town centre at night, full beam gives the best view.
repairNote: Built-up areas at night call for dipped headlights — seen without dazzling.

wrongBelief: Driving through a lit town centre at night, sidelights only are enough.
repairNote: Built-up areas at night call for dipped headlights — seen without dazzling.

wrongBelief: If dazzled by oncoming full beam, you should flash your own full beam back at them.
repairNote: If dazzled, slow down and if necessary stop — never retaliate with your own beam.

wrongBelief: Following another car at night, you should use full beam so they can see further too.
repairNote: Full beam in a following position dazzles through their mirrors — dip it.

wrongBelief: Once fog clears, you may leave your rear fog lights on until you park.
repairNote: Fog lights must go off when visibility improves — they dazzle and hide your brake lights.

wrongBelief: Fog lights make you safer in any rain or drizzle because brighter is always safer.
repairNote: Use fog lights only when visibility is seriously reduced, generally below 100 m.

wrongBelief: Under the hierarchy of road users, pedestrians carry the greatest responsibility since they're most at risk.
repairNote: Greater potential harm brings greater responsibility to reduce danger to others.

wrongBelief: When a pedestrian is waiting to cross, you should turn quickly before they step out.
repairNote: Give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road you turn into or from.

wrongBelief: When a cyclist is going straight on, you should accelerate to turn in ahead of them.
repairNote: Riders going ahead have priority — turning across them causes serious collisions.

wrongBelief: Overtaking a cyclist at 28 mph, leaving at least half a metre is enough space.
repairNote: At least 1.5 m up to 30 mph; leave more room when passing faster.

wrongBelief: The safe way past a horse rider is quickly, to spend less time alongside.
repairNote: Horses spook: under 10 mph and at least 2 m of space.

wrongBelief: Pedestrians only have priority over cars at traffic lights, not at other junctions.
repairNote: At junctions, pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross the road you turn into or from go first.

wrongBelief: Cars have priority over pedestrians at junctions because bigger vehicles go first.
repairNote: At junctions, pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross the road you turn into or from go first.

wrongBelief: The hierarchy of road users says all road users carry exactly equal responsibility.
repairNote: The greatest capacity for harm brings the greatest responsibility.

wrongBelief: A red-bordered triangular sign is an order you must obey.
repairNote: Triangles warn of a hazard ahead. Only circles give orders — a warning tells you to prepare, not obey.

wrongBelief: The crossroads warning triangle means you must give way.
repairNote: It warns that roads cross ahead so you watch both ways; priority is set by separate signs or markings.

wrongBelief: A T-junction warning sign means there is a crossroads ahead.
repairNote: A T-shape warns your road ends at a junction ahead; a plus-shape warns of a crossroads. Read the symbol.

wrongBelief: The road-narrows sign always warns the road narrows on the right only.
repairNote: The arrows show which side narrows — the left, the right, or both. Read the symbol before you commit.

wrongBelief: On a steep downhill you should hold the brakes down all the way to the bottom.
repairNote: Choose a lower gear early so engine braking holds your speed; riding the brakes can overheat and fade them.

wrongBelief: The ice warning sign means the road has been gritted and is safe.
repairNote: It warns the road may be icy or slippery. Slow down and avoid sharp braking, steering or acceleration.

wrongBelief: Every warning sign tells you to do one fixed thing, such as stop.
repairNote: A warning names the hazard ahead; you choose the response for the hazard and the conditions you meet.

wrongBelief: A round sign with a red ring is warning you about a hazard ahead.
repairNote: Circles give orders, not warnings. A red ring means a prohibition — something you must not do.

wrongBelief: A red circle with a white bar means 'no through road'.
repairNote: That sign is 'no entry' — you must not drive past it. 'No through road' is a separate rectangular sign.

wrongBelief: The 'no motor vehicles' sign bans everyone, the same as 'no entry'.
repairNote: It bans motor vehicles only — cyclists and pedestrians may still pass. 'No entry' bans all vehicles.

wrongBelief: The no-overtaking sign is just advice you can ignore if the road looks clear.
repairNote: It is an order: you must not overtake until you pass the sign that ends the restriction.

wrongBelief: A red ring around a number is a minimum speed you must reach.
repairNote: A red ring around a number is a compulsory maximum — never a minimum or a target.

wrongBelief: The 'give priority to oncoming traffic' sign means you have priority.
repairNote: The larger arrow is the oncoming traffic that has priority — you give way. A separate sign gives you priority.

wrongBelief: A solid blue circle is only advice or information you can ignore.
repairNote: Blue circles give positive orders you must follow, such as 'turn left' or 'mini-roundabout'.

wrongBelief: A rectangular sign is giving an order you must obey.
repairNote: Rectangles inform or give directions. Triangles warn and circles order — the oblong just tells you what's there.

wrongBelief: A brown sign is warning you of a hazard at the attraction.
repairNote: Brown signs give tourist directions and information — they never warn of danger.

wrongBelief: A blue sign with a white P means no parking, keep moving.
repairNote: A blue sign with a white P points you TO parking. A parking prohibition is a red-and-blue circular sign.

wrongBelief: A diversion route sign marks a permanent new main road.
repairNote: A diversion is temporary — it routes you around roadworks or a closure, then back to the normal road.

wrongBelief: The white centre line separates lanes travelling in the same direction.
repairNote: The centre line separates traffic flowing in OPPOSITE directions; same-way lanes are split by lane lines.

wrongBelief: You may cross a solid white centre line whenever the road ahead looks clear.
repairNote: Where the line nearest you is solid you must not cross it to overtake — wait until it becomes broken.

wrongBelief: Road markings are only guidance, not rules you can be penalised for.
repairNote: Many markings are legal orders — stop lines, box junctions and solid white lines can all bring a penalty.

wrongBelief: Red and amber showing together means you can move off.
repairNote: Red and amber still means stop — it only tells you green is next. Wait until green shows.

wrongBelief: Amber means speed up to get through before the light turns red.
repairNote: Amber alone means stop at the stop line — carry on only if you've crossed it or stopping would be unsafe.

wrongBelief: A green light means you may enter the junction whatever is happening beyond it.
repairNote: Green means go on only if the way is clear — if your exit is blocked, hold back behind the line.

wrongBelief: A green filter arrow lets you go in any direction, like a full green light.
repairNote: A filter arrow releases only the direction it points; the red still holds every other movement.

wrongBelief: You may cross at flashing red lights once the way looks clear.
repairNote: Flashing red means stop and wait until they stop flashing — a second train or a closing bridge may follow.

wrongBelief: A red X on a gantry closes the whole carriageway, not just the lane below it.
repairNote: Gantry signals are lane-specific — a red X above your lane only closes that lane, so move into an open one.

wrongBelief: A speed shown on a motorway gantry is a minimum you must keep up to.
repairNote: A gantry speed is a temporary maximum, never a minimum — shown in a red ring it's the legal limit.

wrongBelief: You can roll past a STOP sign without stopping when the road looks clear.
repairNote: STOP signs sit where your view is restricted — you must stop at the line every time, then look before emerging.

wrongBelief: If snow or dirt covers a sign's face, there's no way to know what it says.
repairNote: Shape still tells you: the octagon is used for STOP alone, precisely so it can be obeyed when it's obscured.

wrongBelief: A broken white line across a junction means you must stop, like a stop line.
repairNote: Broken means give way — stay behind it and emerge when it's safe. Only a solid stop line means stop every time.

wrongBelief: Long white lines down the middle of the road are just an ordinary lane marking.
repairNote: When the marks are longer than the gaps it's a hazard warning line — a hazard is coming, so don't overtake.

wrongBelief: Stopping briefly on the zigzags at a crossing is fine if you're quick.
repairNote: No parking on zigzags at any time — a parked car hides pedestrians from the drivers approaching the crossing.

wrongBelief: When traffic lights fail, traffic on the main road keeps its priority.
repairNote: Nobody has priority at failed lights — treat it as an unmarked crossroads and be ready to stop.

wrongBelief: Traffic lights and signs override a police officer directing traffic.
repairNote: You must obey a police officer, traffic officer, traffic warden or school crossing patrol — their signals take over.

wrongBelief: A parked car isn't a hazard — it isn't going anywhere.
repairNote: Someone may open a door or step out. Pass parked cars slowly and leave room for a door.

wrongBelief: Watching the vehicle in front closely is all the observation you need.
repairNote: Scan far ahead, close in and behind — the hazard that catches you out is the one you never looked at.

wrongBelief: Children near the road will see your car and wait.
repairNote: Children get absorbed and step out between parked cars. Where they might be, expect them.

wrongBelief: A bus at a stop will wait until you've passed.
repairNote: It may signal and pull out — give way if you safely can, and watch for people crossing in front.

wrongBelief: A cyclist ahead will hold a straight line, so you can pass close.
repairNote: They swerve for potholes, drains and gusts. Hang back and give them room to move out.

wrongBelief: If you can't see at a junction, edging out fast gets it over with.
repairNote: Creep forward until you can see. Traffic can't see you either — if you don't know it's clear, don't go.

wrongBelief: Good reactions make up for not looking far ahead.
repairNote: Reacting quickly still costs you thinking distance. Planning early is what keeps the gap you need.

wrongBelief: Front and rear fog lights do the same job, so it makes no difference which are left on.
repairNote: Front fogs help you see; rear fogs help you be seen — and in clear weather rear fogs read as brake lights.

wrongBelief: In daylight you don't need lights on, however murky it gets.
repairNote: Poor daytime visibility calls for dipped headlights so others can see you — fog lights only below 100 m.

wrongBelief: In fog, sitting close behind the tail lights ahead is the safest way to keep your place.
repairNote: That driver sees hazards as late as you do and may stop suddenly. Stay well back.

wrongBelief: In fog you can hold your normal speed as long as you concentrate hard.
repairNote: Drive at a speed you could stop within the distance you can see to be clear.

wrongBelief: Fog only means taking a bit more care — nothing else about the journey changes.
repairNote: Allow more time, clean your windows and lights, and consider whether the journey is essential.

wrongBelief: Bad weather adds a bit to your stopping distance, whether it is wet or icy.
repairNote: Wet roughly doubles it; ice can multiply it by ten — the two are nothing like each other.

wrongBelief: On ice you just need a slightly bigger gap than usual.
repairNote: Leave up to ten times the normal gap — on ice a small increase is nowhere near enough.

wrongBelief: While tyres are above the legal tread limit they stop you just as well.
repairNote: Tread depth and pressure change your braking distance long before a tyre becomes illegal.

wrongBelief: Steering that goes light on a wet road means the car is handling well.
repairNote: It means the tyres are floating on water. Ease off the accelerator; do not brake until the steering feels normal.

wrongBelief: If someone pulls into the gap you left, close it back up to keep your place.
repairNote: You've lost your stopping distance, not your place in a queue — ease back until the gap is safe again.

wrongBelief: Rolling in neutral saves fuel and is harmless.
repairNote: Coasting removes engine braking and steering response — less control, and no real benefit.

wrongBelief: The brakes are the only thing that can slow the car down.
repairNote: A lower gear brings engine braking — it slows you, settles the car and saves the brakes.

wrongBelief: On a long descent, holding the brakes on all the way is the safe way down.
repairNote: Select a low gear and use the brakes carefully — continuous braking overheats them and they fade.

wrongBelief: Skids are caused by the weather or the road, not by the driver.
repairNote: The driver causes the skid — braking, steering or accelerating too harshly for the grip available.

wrongBelief: On ice, pull away in a low gear with plenty of revs to get moving.
repairNote: Use the highest gear you can and a light foot — power at the wheels is what spins them.

wrongBelief: You can always see when a road is icy.
repairNote: Ice can look like damp tarmac. Near-silent tyres and light steering are the warning you get.

wrongBelief: Eating a big meal or sticking to one drink keeps you fit to drive later.
repairNote: Nothing speeds alcohol out of your body. If you are driving later in the day, drink none at all.

wrongBelief: You can tell when alcohol is affecting your driving, so you'd compensate for it.
repairNote: Alcohol raises confidence while cutting judgement — the impairment hides itself from you.

wrongBelief: Fresh air, loud music or driving slower will get you through a spell of drowsiness.
repairNote: Those buy seconds, not alertness. Stop and rest as soon as you safely can.

wrongBelief: If you get tired on a motorway you can pull onto the hard shoulder for a rest.
repairNote: The hard shoulder is for emergencies only. Leave at the next exit or services, then rest.

wrongBelief: Medicine you can buy without a prescription can't affect your driving.
repairNote: Cough and cold remedies cause drowsiness too. Check the label, and ask your doctor if unsure.

wrongBelief: Glasses you need for driving are only needed at night or in bad weather.
repairNote: If you need them to read a number plate at the required distance, you must wear them whenever you drive.

wrongBelief: A quick glance at a map or phone between mirror checks is safe enough.
repairNote: Nothing may take your attention off the road. Stop somewhere safe and check it there.

wrongBelief: At an unmarked crossroads the wider or busier road has priority.
repairNote: No-one has priority at an unmarked crossroads. Slow down, look both ways and be ready to give way.

wrongBelief: Whoever reaches an unmarked crossroads first can go through.
repairNote: Arriving first gives you nothing. Nobody has priority, so make sure the other driver has seen you.

wrongBelief: Once you've started turning right, oncoming traffic has to wait for you.
repairNote: Oncoming traffic keeps priority until you're across. Wait for a gap you're certain of before you commit.

wrongBelief: When parked cars narrow the road, whoever reaches the gap first goes through.
repairNote: If the obstruction is on your side, give way to oncoming traffic — arriving first changes nothing.

wrongBelief: You can always wait in the central reservation until the far carriageway clears.
repairNote: Only if your whole vehicle fits in the gap. If it doesn't, wait until both carriageways are clear.

wrongBelief: A flash of headlights is another driver inviting you to pull out.
repairNote: Flashing headlights only means 'I am here'. Never move off on someone else's flash without checking yourself.

wrongBelief: A roundabout sign means you have priority through the junction ahead.
repairNote: It only warns you a roundabout is coming. On it, you give way to traffic from your immediate right.

wrongBelief: A mini-roundabout is a one-way system you can enter from any side.
repairNote: It's a roundabout like any other: approach it the same way and give way to traffic from your right.

wrongBelief: The painted circle at a mini-roundabout is just a marking you can drive straight over.
repairNote: Drive round the circle. Only vehicles physically too long to do so may pass over it.

wrongBelief: You always join a roundabout in the left-hand lane, whichever exit you want.
repairNote: Left lane for left or straight ahead; right lane, signalling right, when you're turning right.

wrongBelief: A long vehicle's position on the road tells you which exit it's taking.
repairNote: Long vehicles swing wide to get round. Read the indicators, not the position, and keep well back.

wrongBelief: Being already on a roundabout means you can cross to your exit without checking behind.
repairNote: Mirror and blind spot first — cyclists and riders often stay left all the way round, on your inside.

wrongBelief: Flashing amber at a pelican crossing means go.
repairNote: Give way to anyone still on the crossing; go only when it's clear.

wrongBelief: Every light-controlled crossing has a flashing-amber phase.
repairNote: A puffin has none: sensors hold the red while people cross, then a steady amber follows the green.

wrongBelief: Cyclists may ride across any pedestrian crossing.
repairNote: Only a toucan is shared. At a pelican or puffin a cyclist should get off and push across.

wrongBelief: Someone waiting at a zebra crossing can be ignored until they step out.
repairNote: You MUST give way once they're on the crossing, and you should give way to anyone waiting to cross.

wrongBelief: Waving a pedestrian across is polite if you've checked your mirrors.
repairNote: Never wave anyone across. Your mirrors can't see what an overtaking driver is about to do.

wrongBelief: You may overtake a car stopped at a crossing if the crossing looks clear from where you are.
repairNote: Never overtake the vehicle nearest a crossing. It's stopped because it can see something you can't.

wrongBelief: Queuing across a pedestrian crossing is fine as long as you keep moving with the traffic.
repairNote: Stop before the crossing and leave it clear, even if it opens a gap in the queue.

wrongBelief: If you're in the wrong lane at a junction, cut across into the right one.
repairNote: Stay in your lane and find another way round. A last-moment change is how side-swipes happen.

wrongBelief: The right-hand lane of a dual carriageway is the fast lane, for anyone in a hurry.
repairNote: It's for overtaking or turning right. Move back to the left as soon as you've finished.

wrongBelief: You may only ever overtake on the right, including in a one-way street.
repairNote: In a one-way street all the traffic runs the same way, so you may pass on either side.

wrongBelief: You may drive in a cycle lane when no cyclist is using it.
repairNote: A solid white line means keep out while the lane is operating, empty or not.

wrongBelief: You may use a bus lane whenever there's no bus in sight.
repairNote: The sign gives the hours it operates. Outside those hours you may use it; inside them you may not.

wrongBelief: Move out to the middle of the road before turning left, so you can swing in.
repairNote: Keep well to the left. Swinging out opens a gap a cyclist or moped can ride straight into.

wrongBelief: Signalling to change lane makes the space yours.
repairNote: A signal is information, not a claim. Mirror, blind spot, then move only into a gap that's really there.

wrongBelief: A steady amber at a level crossing means hurry across before the red lights start.
repairNote: Amber is the first warning of a train. Stop, unless you've already crossed the white line.

wrongBelief: You can cross while the barrier is still up, even once the red lights are flashing.
repairNote: Flashing red means stop, whatever the barrier is doing. The lights start well before the train arrives.

wrongBelief: Once a train has passed the crossing is safe to cross.
repairNote: If the lights are still flashing, another train is coming. Wait until they stop.

wrongBelief: If the warning starts while you're on a level crossing, stop and wait for the barrier.
repairNote: Keep going and clear the crossing. Never stop on the rails.

wrongBelief: White boards with red diagonal bars beside the road are roadworks markers.
repairNote: They count down to a concealed level crossing — three bars, two, one.

wrongBelief: If no lights are flashing you can drive straight onto a level crossing.
repairNote: The far side has to be clear too, so nothing can leave you stopped on the rails.

wrongBelief: If people are already crossing a side road you can steer round behind them.
repairNote: Once they've started to cross they have priority — wait until they're clear of the road.

wrongBelief: The safest way past roadworks is to keep your speed up and get clear of them.
repairNote: A closed pavement puts people in the road — slow down and expect them to be walking there.

wrongBelief: On a road with no pavement, walkers keep to the left like the traffic does.
repairNote: Without a pavement they walk on the right, facing traffic — so they meet you head-on.

wrongBelief: The red band on a white stick is just a reflective strip; the person is blind.
repairNote: The red band means deaf as well as blind — they can neither see you nor hear your horn.

wrongBelief: A dog in a yellow or burgundy coat belongs to a trainer out working with a puppy.
repairNote: That coat marks an assistance dog for a deaf owner, who may not hear you coming.

wrongBelief: Once the crossing light turns green the road is yours and pedestrians should hurry.
repairNote: Green means go only when the crossing is clear. Wait for anyone still on it, however slow.

wrongBelief: A school crossing patrol is only advising you to stop, so you can creep past when it looks clear.
repairNote: Their 'stop' sign is an order. Stop, and stay stopped until they're back on the pavement.

wrongBelief: Flashing amber lights under a school sign only remind you that a school is somewhere nearby.
repairNote: They're switched on because children may be crossing now — cut your speed until you're clear.

wrongBelief: You may stop on the school zigzags to drop off or pick up children.
repairNote: No waiting or parking on them at all — they keep the crossing point visible from both sides.

wrongBelief: Your mirrors show you everything you need to see before you reverse.
repairNote: A small child or a low obstruction sits entirely below the glass. If you can't be sure, get out and look.

wrongBelief: Anyone standing behind your car would show up in the rear window before you moved.
repairNote: Children are the hardest road users to see when reversing — they can be completely hidden.

wrongBelief: A pedestrian will wait for you to finish reversing before they cross behind you.
repairNote: Stop and give way to anyone wanting to cross behind you, and never wave them past.

wrongBelief: If the road looked clear when you first looked, it's safe to pull out of the side road.
repairNote: A motorbike can sit entirely behind a parked van or a pillar. Look a second time, for the small shape.

wrongBelief: Windscreen pillars are too narrow to hide anything that matters.
repairNote: At bends and junctions a pillar can hide a whole rider, cyclist or pedestrian. Move your head and look past it.

wrongBelief: At a junction you're looking for cars; anything smaller you'd notice anyway.
repairNote: Bikes are exactly what drivers miss. Take particular care to look for motorcyclists and cyclists at junctions.

wrongBelief: Once your right-turn signal is on, nobody will try to overtake you.
repairNote: A rider may not have seen it. Check the right mirror and blind spot again just before you turn.

wrongBelief: In slow-moving queued traffic nothing can be moving between the lanes.
repairNote: Motorcyclists filter past on either side. Mirror and blind-spot check before every lane change.

wrongBelief: A rider glancing over their shoulder is just shifting their weight to keep balance.
repairNote: It's a blind-spot check, and it usually means they're about to change direction.

wrongBelief: A motorcycle showing a headlight in daylight is inviting you to pull out in front of it.
repairNote: The headlight is there to make the rider easier to see, never as a signal to you.

wrongBelief: A cyclist in the left-hand lane approaching a roundabout must be turning left.
repairNote: They may keep left the whole way round and still be turning right. Expect any direction.

wrongBelief: A cyclist signalling right at a roundabout needs you to wave them across.
repairNote: Never signal them across. Hold back and leave them the room to take their own line.

wrongBelief: A horse rider keeping to the left at a roundabout will be leaving at the first exit.
repairNote: Horses often stay left all the way round, whatever the signal says. Stay well back.

wrongBelief: A rider in the middle of a narrow lane is being inconsiderate and should be moved along.
repairNote: Riding centrally makes them visible and stops you squeezing past. Stay behind until it's genuinely safe.

wrongBelief: The marked box between two stop lines is spare space any vehicle may wait in.
repairNote: It's reserved for cyclists. Stop at the first line unless the lights changed as you crossed it.

wrongBelief: A bicycle wheel showing between parked cars is just a bike parked at the kerb.
repairNote: Treat it as a cyclist about to pull out. Slow down and be ready to stop.

wrongBelief: A quick blast of the horn moves loose animals out of your way.
repairNote: Noise frightens them further into the road. Pass very slowly and quietly, ready to stop.

wrongBelief: A long vehicle indicating one way must have signalled wrongly if it moves the other way.
repairNote: It swings out the opposite way first so the trailer clears the kerb. Stay back and give it room.

wrongBelief: Tucking in close behind a lorry gives you a better view of the road past it.
repairNote: The closer you are, the less you see — and the driver loses you from their mirrors. Drop back.

wrongBelief: If a driver takes the gap you left, close up so it can't happen again.
repairNote: That gap is your stopping room. Ease off and rebuild it rather than defending it.

wrongBelief: Moving closer to a lorry keeps you out of the worst of its spray.
repairNote: Closer means less spray but far less view. Drop back until you can see the road again.

wrongBelief: People getting off a bus will walk to a crossing before stepping into the road.
repairNote: They step straight out from in front of and behind the bus, hidden until the last moment.

wrongBelief: A bus signalling to leave a stop has to wait for all the passing traffic.
repairNote: Give way to it when you safely can, rather than accelerating to get past.

wrongBelief: Staying close behind a hesitant learner encourages them to get on with it.
repairNote: Pressure makes mistakes more likely. Hang back and give them time and room.
